text: The answer depended on one man and one place. The man was Oliver Smith. Quiet. Methodical. A pipe smoker who rarely raised his voice. Some of his officers called him the Professor. The place was Hagaru-ri. Hagaru-ri sat at the southern tip of the reservoir. It was the hub of the entire campaign. Supplies. Fuel. Ammunition. A field hospital. And the airstrip Smith had ordered weeks earlier. On the night of November twenty-eighth it was held by a single understrength Marine battalion under Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Ridge. He had only a few thousand men to defend a perimeter about four miles around. Truck drivers and engineers and clerks were handed rifles and sent to the line. The Chinese struck from the southwest and from a height the Marines called East Hill. They broke into the perimeter more than once. Each time they were pushed back. Engineers fought through the night and climbed back onto their bulldozers at dawn. The airstrip was everything. Without it the wounded would die and the division would have no lifeline. The engineers kept working around the clock under floodlights even as enemy fire swept across the field. The ground was so hard it fought every blade. They kept going. On December first the first transport plane landed on the half-finished strip. Over the following days aircraft lifted out more than four thousand wounded and frostbitten men. They flew in ammunition and medical supplies. They flew in replacements. For the men surrounded on that plateau the sound of those engines meant hope. Meanwhile Smith made the most important decision of the campaign. The division would come out together. All of it. Every man who could walk. Every wounded Marine who could not. As much equipment as the trucks could carry. Nothing that could help the enemy would be left behind. There was talk of flying the Marines out and abandoning their equipment. Smith would not hear of it. They would walk out as a fighting division. It was during these days at Hagaru-ri that reporters asked Smith if the Marines were retreating. His answer became legend. The newspapers reported it in four famous words and a promise. Retreat, hell! We're just attacking in another direction. Historians still debate his exact words. Smith later explained what he meant. When you are surrounded there is no rear. There is nowhere to retreat to. You can only break out. But the meaning was the same either way. The Marines would not run. They would fight their way out. First the regiments at Yudam-ni had to reach him. On December first they began their breakout. Fourteen miles. Wounded men were strapped to trucks and tanks and the hoods of jeeps. Some of the dead were carried too. And between them and Hagaru-ri sat Toktong Pass.
